name: bakers frosting
instructions:
Old-fashioned baker's frosting — like buttercream in structure, but with CRISCO instead of butter, WATER instead of dairy, and CREAM OF TARTAR for tanginess. Shelf-stable at room temperature. What professional bakeries have used historically for decorated / piped work where dairy-based buttercream would slump.

Beat vegetable shortening (Crisco) until smooth. Gradually add powdered sugar. Add a pinch of cream of tartar (for tanginess — the tang that dairy would otherwise contribute) and a pinch of salt. Add WATER a tablespoon at a time until you hit the desired texture — less for stiff piping, more for spreading.

CRITICAL — ADD FAT SLOWLY / INCREMENTALLY: same rule as buttercream. If the shortening's on the soft side, add it to the powdered sugar incrementally rather than dumping it all in. Too much fat overwhelms the sugar and tips the frosting from matte-fluffy into shiny/greasy — one-way trip.
notes:
=== WHAT THIS IS — OLD-FASHIONED BAKER'S FROSTING ===

Old-fashioned recipe. What professional bakeries have used historically for decorated cakes / piped work / anything that needs to sit out under lights for hours. The crisco + water + cream of tartar combination is what makes it shelf-stable in a way dairy buttercream isn't.

Split out from buttercream-frosting — used to live there as a Crisco variant. It's a distinct-enough dish (different fat, different liquid, different tang mechanism) to be its own recipe.

=== CRISCO (VEGETABLE SHORTENING) INSTEAD OF BUTTER — SHELF STABLE ===

Crisco (or similar vegetable shortening) has no dairy — that's why it doesn't slump at room temp the way butter does, and why it doesn't go off if left out for hours. This is one of the few applications where vegetable shortening is genuinely the right pick — most baking wants butter as the flavor and dairy-fat carrier, but here the goal is structural stability more than butter flavor.

=== WATER INSTEAD OF DAIRY ===

Water instead of milk or cream. Dairy would defeat the whole point (add the slump-and-spoil problem back in). Water hydrates the frosting to the right consistency without introducing anything perishable.

=== CREAM OF TARTAR FOR TANGINESS ===

The tang that dairy would normally contribute (buttercream's butter has a bit; cream cheese frosting's cream cheese has a lot). A pinch of cream of tartar mimics that acidic-tang note without adding any dairy. Not sweet, not sour — just a background acid brightness that keeps the frosting from reading purely fat-and-sugar.

=== WHEN TO REACH FOR THIS ===

- A cake that'll sit on a table at a party / event for hours.
- A cake being transported (car, cooler, etc.) where fridge access isn't guaranteed.
- Detailed piping / decorative work that needs to hold shape.
- Any occasion where you'd normally worry about a buttercream slumping.

For eat-immediately service, straight buttercream-frosting (real butter, dairy) has better flavor. Bakers frosting wins on stability, buttercream wins on flavor.

=== TRADEOFF — LESS DAIRY FLAVOR ===

The stability comes at the cost of butter flavor. If you want SOME butter flavor plus SOME stability, a 50/50 buttercream/bakers-frosting split works (half butter, half crisco; half milk, half water; same cream of tartar) — but that's a hybrid, not the pure old-fashioned baker's version.

=== SHELF-STABILITY RANKING (CAKE TOPPINGS) ===

Shelf-stable (can sit out at room temp for hours): bakers-frosting (best of the class — the whole point), buttercream-frosting.

Not shelf-stable (need refrigeration): cream-cheese-frosting, strawberry-compote.

Middle: chocolate-ganache — technically not shelf-stable due to the cream, but more stable than cream cheese frosting or compote.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- buttercream-frosting: dairy-based sibling. Better flavor; slumps at room temp; needs refrigeration for long sits.
- cream-cheese-frosting: softer and tangier from the cream cheese; needs refrigeration.
- caramel-frosting: caramelized dairy alternative.
- chocolate-ganache: chocolate + cream, looser format.
